1.pericope_label: Saul’s standing army, Jonathan’s blow at Geba, the Philistine muster and Israel in the caves

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that the only possible literal rendering of the opening is that Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign, that the corruption or gap in the text dates from a far back period, and that the English version is simply a probable but conjectural paraphrase; he notes that the Chaldee and some of the Rabbis interpret it of Saul as an innocent child, and that in several places in these books the numbers are quite untrustworthy. The three thousand men he calls a very important statement, telling of the first beginning of a standing army in Israel and the first step towards her becoming a great military power: it was Saul’s military genius and foresight that enabled David and Solomon to make the conquests which raised Israel for a time among the greatest of Eastern powers, while Saul’s own great life was frittered away repelling domestic enemies. Of the Philistine host he says the figures are perfectly untrustworthy, arguing from the rolls of ancient armies, in which the war chariots are always fewer than the horsemen, whereas here they are made four times as numerous. Keil and Delitzsch meet the opening difficulty from the form of words instead: by the standing custom in the history of the kings such a notice opens with the king’s age at his accession and the length of his reign, and comparison with the accession formulas of Ishbosheth and David and the kings of Judah leaves no doubt that this verse was meant to do the same, so that a number has dropped out. Of the flight they render the list of hiding places as caves, thorn-bushes, clefts of the rocks and fortresses.

Gill collects three readings of the opening clause: that Saul had a son a year old when he began to reign, namely Ishbosheth, who was forty when his father died; that there is an ellipsis of the number, to be supplied as thirty or forty; or that the words are figurative, of one like a child of a year old for purity and innocence. He supplies the arithmetic of the levy, that the three thousand were drawn from the three hundred thousand who had gone against the Ammonites, some appointed as a guard about Saul’s person and the rest kept as a standing force. On the garrison Jonathan smote he argues against Jarchi that Geba is not the same place as Gibeah of Benjamin, since it can hardly be thought Jonathan would station himself with his thousand men where the Philistines had a garrison, and he follows Kimchi in making them two places, both in Benjamin and probably not far apart. He reports that Abarbinel refers the clause about the people being distressed not to Israel but to the other side.

Clarke reads the three thousand tactically, that Saul divided them and sent them against the garrisons at Michmash and Bethel and Gibeah, hoping by surprising them to get swords and spears for his people, of which the chapter later says they were entirely destitute. On the Philistine muster he finds no proportion between the chariots and the cavalry, observes that the largest armies ever brought into the field, even by mighty emperors, were never furnished with thirty thousand chariots, and judges the word for thirty a false reading for three, the Syriac and the Arabic both giving three thousand. The flight he explains by numbers and equipment, that the Israelites were few and totally unarmed as to swords and spears and were terrified at so numerous and well-appointed an army, Judea being full of rocks and caves where men might shelter, so that some hid, others fled beyond Jordan, and those who clave to Saul followed him trembling. Wesley keeps the figure of the chariots and changes the word, supposing most of them carriages for baggage rather than chariots of war.

Henry sets the whole retreat under a judgment: we are not told wherein Israel had offended so as to forfeit God’s presence and turn his hand against them, but doubtless they had left God, else he would not have left them. Saul, he adds, was weak and impolitic and did not order his affairs with discretion; and of the opening clause he notes that the phrase ordinarily dates a man’s birth rather than his reign, which is why some have understood it figuratively of one as innocent and good as a child.

8.pericope_label: Saul sacrifices before Samuel comes, and hears that his kingdom shall not continue

schools.summary: Clarke cuts the chronological knot by denying the obvious reference: what is said here cannot be understood of the order given when Saul was anointed but of a different appointment, Samuel having promised on this occasion to come within seven days and having kept his word, since he arrived before the day was out. He holds the act itself unlawful, calling it most perfectly unconstitutional, since Saul had no authority to offer, or even to cause to be offered, any of the Lord’s sacrifices. Saul’s defence he itemises as three excuses — that the people were fast leaving his standard, that Samuel had not come at the very commencement of the time though he came within it, and that the Philistines were coming fast upon him — and judges that in all this Saul was sincere but rash, and regardless of a precept he had evidently received. Wesley agrees with Gill that the seventh day was not finished, glosses the complaint that Samuel came not as meaning that a good part of the day had passed so that Saul concluded he would not come, takes the admission that he forced himself as against his own mind and inclination, and observes from the mention of supplication that sacrifices were accompanied with solemn prayers. On the sentence he qualifies what was forfeited, noting that the phrase for ever in scripture often signifies only a long time, so that it would have been abundantly verified had the kingdom been enjoyed by Saul and by his son and by his son’s son, after whom it might have come to Judah in any case.

Ellicott feels the difficulty of referring the set time back to the day of Saul’s prophetic consecration, which took place at least three or four years and perhaps much longer before this, especially as the two men had certainly been together at Gilgal in the meantime; yet the extraordinary solemnity of that earlier warning draws him back towards it. On the nature of the sin he denies the common account: many have supposed its greatness lay in Saul’s offering with his own hand, but not a hint of it is anywhere given us, and it is more than probable that the sacrifice, offered so prematurely in the absence of the seer, was performed by the hand of the priest who was no doubt in attendance on the king, so that there was no unlawful assumption of priestly functions. He puts the king’s position bluntly, that Saul would gratefully receive any help the prophet could bring but in such an emergency preferred, sooner than run any risk, to act alone and if necessary to go into battle without divine consecration. Keil and Delitzsch read the Hebrew as Ellicott does, that the phrase does not imply Saul offered with his own hand or performed the priestly function on this occasion; and they supply the fear behind the act, that he resolved to sacrifice without Samuel in his anxiety lest the people lose heart and forsake him altogether if there were further delay.

Henry offers two harmonisations of the appointed time, that the order though recorded earlier may have been given afterwards, or that it was given as a general rule to be observed at every public gathering at Gilgal; and he treats the offence as Saul’s sacrificing before Samuel came, Samuel having promised that at the end of those days he would be sure to come and both offer sacrifices for him and direct him what he should do.

Gill has Saul tarry to the seventh day but not to the end of it, as he should have done, and explains his motive as impatience together with seeing the people desert him apace and being unwilling to engage in battle without first sacrificing to God and imploring his help. He settles the question of the sin from the rebuke itself: Saul is charged with not waiting the full time, which showed his impatience, his disregard to Samuel and his distrust of God, and with intruding into the priest’s office he is not charged. He notices the timing, that Samuel arrived after the burnt offering was ended but before the peace offerings could be offered, and takes the kingdom that shall not continue to mean not in Saul’s family nor in his tribe, but removed to another.

No: not a hint of it is given, and the priest in attendance probably performed it
No: the Hebrew does not imply he performed the priestly function himself
No: with that he is not charged, but with not waiting the full time

Alone in limiting what was forfeited, since "for ever" often means only a long time, which three generations would have verified.

15.pericope_label: Samuel goes up from Gilgal, Saul numbers six hundred men, and the spoilers go out in three companies

schools.summary: Gill sees anger in the manner of Samuel’s going, that he arose seemingly in wrath and displeasure and did not stay to offer the peace offerings which remained, though he thinks Saul followed him, or at least came after him quickly. That the raiders could go out at all he turns into a reproach: Saul did not dare come out to fight and there was none throughout the land to oppose them, so the Philistines sent three companies to ravage and spoil the country — of so little use and service was a king to Israel, which they had been so extremely desirous of, and this was suffered to convince them of their vain confidence. He fixes one of the three roads, that Beth-horon named two cities, the upper and the nether, both in the tribe of Ephraim, lying northwest of the Philistine camp at Michmash and some eight miles from it.

Henry reads the departure as abandonment with a reservation. Saul has set up for himself and is now left to himself, and it does not appear that Samuel either prayed with him or directed him; yet by going up to Gibeah of Benjamin, which was Saul’s own city, he intimated that he had not quite abandoned him but waited to do him a kindness another time — or else, Henry allows, he went to the college of the prophets there, in order to pray for Saul when he did not think fit to pray with him.

Clarke has the two men travel together and makes the journey an act of support: though David in the divine purpose is appointed captain over the people, Saul is not to be removed from the government during his life, and Samuel therefore accompanies him to Gibeah to give him the requisite help in this conjuncture. Of the muster he notes without comment that the six hundred were the whole of the Israelitish army at this time, and not one sword or spear among them. The division of the Philistine force he reads tactically and looks ahead with it, that finding the Israelites durst not risk a battle they split their army in three to pillage and destroy the country, and that Jonathan profited by the circumstance and attacked what remained of the army at Michmash.

Ellicott has Samuel pass from Gilgal alone, but judges that he does not yet break off friendly relations with Saul, and wonders whether the noble old man still hoped the brilliant and gallant king would recognise his fatal error. He then charges the English translators with an outright mistake and diagnoses its cause: Saul and Jonathan, uniting their sadly diminished forces, entrench themselves at Geba, in a strong position at the end of a pass from which they could watch the movements of the Philistines, their small number forbidding any idea of an attack; and where the version reads Gibeah of Benjamin it should read Geba of Benjamin, the translators having probably been led astray by the mention of Gibeah in the preceding verse. Of the raids he cautions that the compiler of these books does not profess to give a detailed account of this or any of Saul’s wars, and supposes the great armed demonstration had completely cowed the Israelites, certainly in the southern part of Canaan. Keil and Delitzsch treat what follows as continuous with this so far as the facts are concerned, holding that the account of Israel’s disarming belongs with the foregoing, since it was Jonathan’s brave heroic deed and the splendid victory it brought that terminated the war for which Saul had entreated help.

Geba: the translators substituted Gibeah, led astray by the preceding verse

Alone in turning the unopposed raids into a reproach against Israel’s demand for a king.

19.pericope_label: No smith in Israel: the Philistine monopoly of iron, and a people with neither sword nor spear

schools.summary: Gill explains the absence of smiths as deliberate policy, that the Philistines while they ruled had removed them into their own country and forbidden any to learn or exercise the trade in Israel, so that the Israelites were obliged to go into Philistia, to one or other of their cities or garrisons, where the trade was exercised. On the disputed word of the following verse he offers a third arrangement besides the two the others canvass, that those who would not go down to the Philistines, or were not able, or thought it too much trouble, kept files by them to sharpen their instruments upon occasion; though he reports that the words are by some joined to the verse before, so that it was to the Philistines they went to sharpen the tools when the edges were blunt.

Clarke thinks the smiths were likely carried off in the former wars, and sets two parallels beside it: Porsenna, in the peace he granted the Romans, permitted no iron to be forged except for the purposes of agriculture, and the Chaldeans did the same to the Jews in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, carrying away all the artificers. He then presses the Roman parallel to mark a difference, finding from this passage that the Philistines did not grant Israel even as much as Porsenna granted Rome, since he at least permitted the people to manufacture the implements of husbandry. On the disputed word he reports that the Hebrew noun, from a root meaning to rub hard, is translated very differently by the versions and by critics, and settles for the received sense as likely as any, that the people were allowed the use of files — though he suspects the word means a grindstone — to restore the blunted edges of their tridents and axes and goads. The statement that no sword or spear was found he treats as an objection to be answered, asking how Israel could be totally destitute of arms if they had enjoyed such profound peace and undisturbed dominion under Samuel, a state which argues the lowest circumstances of oppression and vassalage; and he answers by distinguishing the weapons, since the bow and the sling were the principal arms of Israel and for these they needed no smith at all. Wesley denies that they went to the land of the Philistines at all, taking it of the stations and garrisons the Philistines retained within Israel’s own territory, Samuel’s authority having so far overawed them that they durst not give the Israelites much disturbance; in these, he says, the Philistines kept all the smiths and allowed them the exercise of their art for the uses that follow.

Ellicott limits the claim about the smithies, allowing a year or perhaps two or three to have elapsed while Saul and Jonathan abode in Gibeah and the Philistine raids went on unchecked, and judging that the statement probably refers specially to the southern districts of Canaan. He reaches the same Roman parallel as Clarke, that Porsenna allowed the Romans iron implements for agriculture only. Of the implements themselves he admits defeat, noting that the word rendered coulter is elsewhere given as ploughshare by most of the older versions and that we cannot now distinguish the two with any precision, and that Jerome renders another of them by hoe. On the disputed word he grants that the received rendering is supported by the Targum and by many of the great Hebrew commentators, Rashi among them, but reports that Gesenius and the majority of modern scholars render it instead by bluntness, so that the passage would say there was dulness of edge upon the mattocks and the rest. The absence of arms he says must not be pressed too literally, holding that it was the general result of the raids in the open valleys of southern Canaan, especially the Benjamite territory, which were just the districts from which Saul and Jonathan could most easily have recruited their thinned and dispirited forces. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the inventory, giving the share and coulter, the axe and mattock, and the goads that were sharpened.
